item.title: White House threatens criminal investigation into Democrats’ oversight efforts
item.description: A letter from the Trump administration’s top lawyer accuses Democrats of potentially crossing constitutional guardrails.
item.category: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee

media:content.media:title: House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) speaks with reporters and victims of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein outside a closed interview with former Attorney General Pam Bondi on Capitol Hill on May 29, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette
item.dc:contributor: By Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
The White House’s top lawyer is threatening a criminal investigation of Democrats for conducting what he alleges are illegitimate investigations into the executive branch — a stark escalation from the Trump administration as Congressional Democrats prepare to launch an oversight onslaught when they assume the majority in January.

White House counsel Will Scharf, in a letter to incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia, says Democrats’ repeated public promises to use their new majority to investigate the president and his allies could cross constitutional limits — and even amount to illegal threats.

The letter, dated Monday but publicly revealed Wednesday, informs the California Democrat that the White House is “monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government.”

It also cites several statements from Garcia and his Democratic colleagues, attempting to paint their efforts as unmoored in a legislative purpose and instead as threats “designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear.”

Scharf further warns Garcia that those actions could venture into the realm of “blatant criminality” and could give rise to an investigation by the executive branch into Congress.

The attorney’s comments track closely with social media posts from President Donald Trump, who has suggested Democrats could face criminal consequences for their aggressive posture. It’s a departure from precedent, as the Justice Department is typically the front line for engaging with Congress on matters related to congressional oversight.

At the heart of the White House’s complaint is a legal requirement that congressional subpoenas be rooted in a clear “legislative purpose” and can’t be used simply to harass or intimidate. But courts for decades have afforded great deference to legislative investigators and have refused to delve into the subjective mindset of individual lawmakers when congressional committees act.

A spokesperson for Garcia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Capitol agenda: The left looks to Van Hollen for a shake-up
item.description: The 67-year-old Maryland lawmaker has caught the attention of a handful of increasingly vocal progressive lawmakers and activists who say it’s time for Chuck Schumer to step aside.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks with reporters at the U.S. Capitol Dec. 15, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Chris Van Hollen is having a very strange moment.

The 67-year-old Maryland lawmaker has caught the attention of a handful of progressive lawmakers and activists who have gotten increasingly vocal this week that it’s time for Chuck Schumer to step aside as the Senate’s longtime top Democrat.

But Van Hollen has wavered on whether he will challenge Schumer in a race to be majority leader in the aftermath of massive midterm gains. Van Hollen said Tuesday he is “actively listening” to members of the party as he keeps the door open to a role in Senate leadership — or perhaps a 2028 presidential bid.

Schumer appears to have a path to the No. 1 post and said Tuesday he is confident he does. His allies point to his prolific fundraising and leadership experience, and are openly discouraging Van Hollen from even jumping into what could be a highly-divisive race.

“I’m going to vote for Schumer. He helped recruit a great class, and I can’t imagine why you would vote for someone like Van Hollen with no record of doing anything,” Sen. John Fetterman told reporters.

But Schumer began facing pockets of opposition with his ranks this week — giving a potential opening to Van Hollen.

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin, for example, on Tuesday announced publicly they are not committed to backing Schumer as the next leader. Neither identified who they support instead, though both acknowledged Van Hollen is one name in consideration.

It’s the culmination of a remarkable resurgence for Van Hollen, who, over the past two years, has become an increasingly strident critic of the Democratic Party establishment. That’s a somewhat striking position from someone who spent decades dutifully rising through the party establishment and who chaired both the House and Senate campaign committees.

“Van Hollen represents a bridge between the old guard — people who’ve been in office for a long time with a more moderate orientation — and the new generation that is coming into office,” said Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution.

For his part, Van Hollen on Tuesday accused Schumer and the Senate Democratic campaign arm of having “sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC” to oppose more progressive candidates. He’s also become increasingly critical of the U.S. posture toward Israel, joining early Democratic pushes to restrict arms sales to the country.

That outspokenness has gotten Van Hollen noticed on the left, including by newly elected senators like Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan.

“I have been very impressed by Senator Van Hollen’s leadership,” said Flanagan, who has said she will not back Schumer.

What else we’re watching: 

— NVIDIA SCANDAL TILTS CHIP FIGHT: The espionage scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is threatening one of the chipmaker’s biggest priorities: stopping new U.S. restrictions on its sales to China. Per lawmakers, congressional aides and lobbyists close to the debate, the revelation that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy has significantly raised the chances Congress will enact chip export limits as part of its must-pass annual defense package, which is being negotiated in the lame-duck session. Speaker Mike Johnson on Tuesday told POLITICO that he supported including export controls in the legislation, echoing Hakeem Jeffries. Senate Banking member Kevin Cramer, meanwhile, called for Huang to resign.

— NEAL PREPS FOR WAYS AND MEANS POST: Rep. Richard Neal is mapping out his oversight and legislative plans as he gears up to lead the powerful tax policy committee. Several new members are poised to join Ways and Means, where Neal has no challengers to his bid for chair. In an exclusive Q&A chat with POLITICO, Neal said the scale of Democrats’ win “mightily” influenced his thinking about how he’ll lead Ways and Means starting next January. When selecting new members, he says he wants to ensure there are voices for “parts of the country that have been shut out in the past.”

Jordain Carney, Kelsey Brugger, Ari Hawkins and Gabby Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: The new darling of the Democratic left is … Chris Van Hollen?
item.description: After decades navigating the Democratic establishment, the Maryland senator has emerged as a face of its resistance.

media:content.media:title: "We should bring a little more democracy to the United States Senate," Chris Van Hollen told activists Tuesday.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney and Calen Razor
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney and Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Progressive lawmakers and activists are hoping to harness momentum from last week’s sweeping Democratic victories to install inspiring new congressional leaders.

Many have looked at the Senate and found their guy: a 67-year-old father of three from an affluent Washington suburb who has held public office continuously since 1991.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has emerged as the alternative of choice for a swath of Democrats who believe Chuck Schumer, the longtime Senate Democratic leader, should step aside despite presiding over massive midterm gains.

It’s the culmination of a remarkable resurgence for Van Hollen, who spent years inching up the Democratic leadership ladder in the House only to ditch his seniority there for the back benches of the Senate in 2017.

Over the past two years, he has emerged as an increasingly strident critic of the Democratic party establishment and its approach to President Donald Trump, as well as its positions on populist economic policies and the U.S. relationship with Israel — and members of the party’s left flank have noticed.

A wave of House Democrats, outside activists and even at least one newly elected senator are effectively trying to draft him into what could be an uphill race to unseat the 75-year-old Schumer as majority leader.

“I have been very impressed by Senator Van Hollen’s leadership,” said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, who beat a more centrist Democrat in her state’s primary and has said she will not back Schumer.

Van Hollen has wavered on whether he is pursuing a role in Senate leadership or perhaps instead a 2028 run for the presidency. He said Tuesday he is “actively listening” as he keeps the door open to a majority leader bid ahead of the early December caucus elections.

“I’m trying to talk to our members, and I think it’s important to reach out to everybody,” he said in the Capitol halls.

Flanagan said she had not had “formal conversations” with Van Hollen, but another younger Democrat — Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan — met with him this week as she called for a leadership shakeup.

Outside the building, at a gathering of progressive groups charting an agenda for the coming Democratic majorities, Van Hollen was sharply critical of the existing Senate Democratic power structure — and Schumer in particular.

“We just saw democracy in America in action — we should bring a little more democracy to the United States Senate,” he said, before later accusing Schumer and the Senate Democratic campaign arm of having “sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC” to oppose more progressive candidates in this year’s primaries.

That outspokenness has gotten Van Hollen noticed on the left — and it has been especially striking coming from a son of prominent U.S. diplomats who spent decades dutifully rising through the Democratic Party establishment and chaired both the House and Senate campaign committees.

“Van Hollen represents a bridge between the old guard — people who’ve been in office for a long time with a more moderate orientation — and the new generation that is coming into office,” said Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution.

His rhetoric and actions have evolved dramatically, however, since Trump returned to office in 2025. The administration’s spending cuts decimated Van Hollen’s constituency — particularly in his political base of Montgomery County — and his posts on the Appropriations and Foreign Relations committees gave him a front-row seat to Trump’s elimination of USAID.

Meanwhile, he became an outspoken critic of the White House’s mass deportation agenda and was the first U.S. lawmaker to visit the El Salvador prison where the administration was sending scores of deportees — including a Maryland man, Kilmar Ábrego García, who had been mistakenly deported in contravention of a court order.

Van Hollen has also become increasingly critical of the U.S. posture toward Israel, joining early Democratic pushes to restrict arms sales to Benjamin Netanyahu’s government as its war on Gaza after the 2023 Hamas attacks grew increasingly brutal.

“He’s been correct,” said Jeff Cohen, founder of RootsAction, a group pushing its members to back Van Hollen over Schumer. “He’s been with the base of the party on most issues: redefining the U.S.-Israel relationship is one. Taxing the wealthy is another, standing up to AI — all of these issues that Schumer is wrong on.”

Van Hollen’s approach to the Senate leadership race has evolved in recent days. He downplayed a bid for top leader earlier this year, including saying in a recent interview that it has “not been my focus.” The day after the election, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed appeared to believe he had passed on a run, calling Van Hollen “my white whale” in response to a question about his ideal Senate leader.

But asked about the matter Tuesday as the drumbeat for his candidacy grew, Van Hollen said there should not be a “coronation” for Schumer as he described his ongoing listening tour.

“We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan and as you know, there are many people who think that a change is required,” he said.

A Senate aide who was granted anonymity to describe Van Hollen’s thinking said the senator has been influenced by the scale of his party’s midterm victory and the calls he has heard for change — as well as the public outreach he is getting. The aide said Van Hollen is not coordinating the outside effort to nudge him into challenging Schumer.

Senate Democrats still broadly expect Schumer to be reelected as leader, and some are openly warning Van Hollen away from jumping into the race.

“I'm going to vote for Schumer. He helped recruit a great class, and I can't imagine why you would vote for someone like Van Hollen with no record of doing anything,” pro-Israel Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) told reporters.

Asked about whether Van Hollen will run, Fetterman added, “I dare him to.”

Schumer’s backers point to his decades of fundraising experience, deep well of relationships within the caucus and across the party, and his work to unite his colleagues and battle Trump over the past year. And with Democrats poised to pick up as many as nine seats — a once-unthinkable outcome — they are questioning why senators would depose the leader who helped make it happen.

"When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract,” Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said Tuesday at a joint news conference with Schumer.

But those arguments are carrying little water with those who view Schumer as out of touch with the direction of the party. They note that while he supported the incoming freshmen with hundreds of millions of dollars of general-election spending, he opposed some of them during the primary.

Van Hollen could be using his flirtations with a bid to influence some end-of-year decisionmaking. He is pushing Congress to cut off Iran war funding as they head toward a Dec. 11 government funding deadline, and he wants a provision mandating cooperation with Israel stripped from the annual defense policy bill.

Those stances could help push Schumer and the party into a more confrontational posture, which Van Hollen signaled he wanted in an interview earlier this year.

“It’s going to be very important that Democrats let voters know not only what we’re against but what we stand for,” he said. “And I think a lot of voters, you know, think Democrats have been too much finger-in-the-wind. They’ve been too wishy-washy.”

Grace Yarrow and Lisa Kashinsky contributed to this report.

item.title: Democrats are going all in on finishing the Epstein investigation
item.description: A POLITICO Poll found more voters want Democrats to pursue an affordability agenda than keep looking into the influence web surrounding the late, convicted sex offender.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) speaks alongside other House Oversight Democrats after they walked out of a briefing from Justice Department officials on the investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on Capitol Hill on March 18, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
House Democrats say they have unfinished business in regards to the Jeffrey Epstein investigation, and they believe their base is counting on them to deliver.

It’s a mandate they are taking even more seriously after last week’s wave election that will give Democrats their biggest majority in decades — and further reinforced by the Tuesday release of a Republican report that purported to close the book on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee’s 15-month investigation into the late, convicted sex offender.

“Our work is just getting started,” Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the incoming Oversight Committee chair, said in a statement. He decried the GOP report as “based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings” as the Justice Department “continues to illegally withhold over 2.5 million pages of documents.”

Democrats are now talking about recalling witnesses to testify under oath and issuing subpoenas to major banks that helped finance Epstein’s trafficking of young women and girls for years.

They are also suggesting there’s more to investigate surrounding Epstein’s relationship with President Donald Trump, and what DOJ might be hiding to protect him.

“So many survivors have called our office or found me in the grocery store, and [said], ‘you know, I wasn't a victim of Epstein, but I've been a victim, and this gives me peace and a sense of justice,’” said Rep. Emily Randall (D-Wash.), a member of the Oversight Committee, of how her constituents are clamoring for a congressional investigation that brings justice to Epstein’s victims by exposing the web of powerful people who enabled his abuse.

But Democrats are also under pressure over the next two years to show they can do more than just conduct oversight of the Trump administration. That includes making good on the campaign promise that united the party in key races around the country: improving affordability and lowering the costs of everyday goods.

Reinforcing voters’ desire to see Congress legislate on pocketbook issues, recent POLITICO Poll findings show that, among those who voted for Democrats in the midterms, 71% said that, when forced to choose, they preferred to the party prioritize bringing down the cost of living — compared to 25% who said they preferred the party continue investigating Epstein.

Progressive Democrats were slightly more likely to prioritize the Epstein files at 31% when faced with that same choice, with moderate Democrats at 21%.

Some Democrats have said in recent days they are worried their leadership will find it easier to wield their new subpoena power than pass laws with Trump still in the White House and plan to push for a legislative agenda the party can run on in 2028.

They also could be turned off by Democrats’ efforts to keep trying to implicate the president in Epstein’s misconduct. Trump has denied wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, and no evidence has suggested he took part in Epstein’s crimes. However, incoming Judiciary Chair Jamie Raskin released a late-October report calling for a special counsel to investigate whether the president sexually assaulted a handful of women in Epstein’s orbit.

And Garcia, in his statement Tuesday, committed to “hold[ing] real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump.”

The Republican committee report, in its summary of findings, accused Democrats of “concentrat[ing] their investigative efforts on President Trump rather than the broader, decades long institutional failures that enabled Epstein’s abuse and robbed survivors of swift justice.”

But Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), who also sits on the Oversight Committee, said that a continuation of the congressional Epstein investigation is actually exactly what voters asked for when they rejected Republicans at the polls last week.

“You essentially have all the problems people are concerned about in one thing: elites, billionaires, politicians getting away with crime because they have money and because they have political power,” Frost said in an interview. “Getting through this is not just going to help us have accountability for what wrongs have been done, but help us understand what more do we need to do as legislators to form legislation so it never happens again.”

Another Oversight Democrat, Rep. Wesley Bell of Missouri, also pointed to voters’ desire to see their elected officials hold powerful people to account: “Rooting out the corruption, getting to the bottom of this investigation that involves likely the largest sex trafficking scheme that this nation — maybe the world — has seen … that's exactly what Americans want us to do.”

In the meantime, Democrats are pledging to plow ahead. Members are also still waiting to get the full slate of documents mandated by the law Congress passed nearly unanimously on Nov. 19, 2025. A top priority in the new Congress will likely be calling in Attorney General Todd Blanche, who oversaw the haphazard release of the Epstein files when he was still deputy to his ousted predecessor, Pam Bondi.

Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), who also sits on the panel, said she and her colleagues have a list of financial institutions that need to be scrutinized for their ties to Epstein. She cited Deutsche Bank and JPMorgan Chase as “the top ones,” but added, “there’s a lot of them.”

Ansari also defended Democrats’ decision to continue the Epstein inquiry in the new Congress despite a loaded legislative and investigative agenda across other committees and issue areas.

“There's one thing that I learned through this process, and even talking with the survivors — every interview you do and every piece of it you learn about, it just has become clear how vast this network was and the entire operation was,” she said. 

“And there's been so much coverup for so many years that I do think this is going to be a years-long endeavor to really get to the truth,” Ansari continued, “and will require a Department of Justice that is focused on it to take it to the point of real accountability.”

item.title: Madeleine Dean ‘considering’ Senate bid against Fetterman
item.description: The two faced off for lieutenant governor in 2018.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) arrives for a House Judiciary Committee markup on Capitol Hill on June 2, 2022.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Pennsylvania Democratic Rep. Madeleine Dean is “considering” a run for Senate in 2028 — including in a potential primary against incumbent Sen. John Fetterman.

“I’m going to be considering it,” Dean said in an interview Tuesday regarding a potential Senate run.

It would be a rematch for Dean, who lost her bid against Fetterman for lieutenant governor in 2018. She went on to be elected to the House later that same year.

“I have been concerned about, really, two things, which is his family and his health … and am very disappointed in his activity as a senator and in his votes,” she said of Fetterman.

It also could put her in a crowded field of Democrats looking to take advantage of Fetterman's diminishing popularity with the party base since his election to the Senate in 2022. He has faced criticism for his prolonged absences from legislative business and support of the Iran war that is out of step with most of the party.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) is among those giving a Senate run “serious thought.”

“When I say consider, nothing is lighthearted,” Dean said of her decision-making process, noting that she came to know and like Fetterman and his wife during the 2018 campaign.

She did not put a timetable on a final verdict, saying she needed to mull it over with her family.

item.title: The incoming Senate Appropriations chair calls for December government funding punt
item.description: Washington Sen. Patty Murray wants a short-term patch to keep federal agencies funded beyond the Dec. 11 shutdown deadline, to give Democrats negotiating leverage when they retake the majority.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) stands for a portrait in her office on Capitol Hill on Nov. 10, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
Federal cash expires in one month, and the Senate Democrat poised to run funding negotiations next year wants a short-term patch into January — when her party takes control.

Looking ahead to the Dec. 11 government shutdown deadline, Washington Sen. Patty Murray said in an interview Tuesday that a stopgap is the best way to ensure Congress passes final, full-year spending bills that fulfill the demands of voters who overwhelmingly chose Democrats on Election Day.

“Voters handed us a huge mandate to write these bills that reflect their priorities,” said Murray, the incoming Senate Appropriations chair. “So how we can lower costs and end corruption and end the war in Iran — the best way for us to do that is to do a short-term CR and then write these funding bills for next year.”

Murray said she wants to boost nondefense dollars for priorities like childcare, education and infrastructure next year, while reining in defense spending and cracking down on President Donald Trump’s moves to shirk Congress’ funding power.

Democrats are still discussing how they might use the December government shutdown deadline to end the Iran conflict, she added — including whether the party will cut off cash for the military operation as a condition of voting to keep federal operations afloat.

“The devil will be in the details,” Murray said, adding that Democrats are “looking at all the options” for ending the war.

Democrats will also demand that any December funding bill extend language blocking the Trump administration from finalizing its plans to put political appointees in charge of approving federal grants, Murray said. Then, when her party takes control of both the House and Senate in January, the new majority will insert new provisions into funding bills designed to stop Trump from shifting, withholding and canceling federal spending Congress mandates.

That includes blocking the president from unilaterally canceling billions of dollars next fall, like he did again this year, and holding oversight hearings to probe the administration's spending tactics, Murray said: “I am going to make sure that we Trump-proof every one of our bills that we write next year, so this administration follows the letter of the law."

Murray, who is currently the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, is expected to wield the gavel next year alongside Sen. Lisa Murkowski in the top Republican spot. The Alaska lawmaker is a longtime friend of Murray's — and a partner over the last two years in pushing back against Trump's moves to claw back funding Congress already approved.

“She and I have a really good friendship,” Murray said of Murkowski. “We have a good, productive and strong working relationship. And I think she will represent her caucus well and be willing to work with us on any differences."

item.title: John Thune says he won’t take sides in 2028 presidential race
item.description: Several Senate Republicans are expected to eye national campaigns.

media:content.media:title: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) speaks with reporters outside his office at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 30, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Tuesday he will not get involved in the GOP’s 2028 presidential primary as several Republican senators consider launching runs to succeed Donald Trump.

“I’m not going to take sides because we’ll have, probably, several senators maybe in that conversation,” Thune said in an interview.

Thune’s comments came after he was reelected to lead the Senate Republicans as they head into the minority come January.

The party’s sweeping loss could remake the 2028 presidential field by taking some shine off Vice President JD Vance’s prospects.

Now some Republicans believe the field could be more open. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who ran in 2016, is flirting with another White House run. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) appeared to reopen the door this week in the wake of the election. Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), another 2016 hopeful, and Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) have also discussed possible bids.

In addition to the White House contenders, Thune will have to accommodate senators who seek reelection in 2028 — on what is viewed as a favorable map for Democrats.

Thune himself could be among them. He told POLITICO earlier this year that his “assumption” was he will seek reelection in 2028.

Asked in an interview Tuesday if the midterm results had impacted his thinking, Thune said he is “gearing up and getting things ready and in position, and we’ll probably be making some announcements about that here soon.”

item.title: What the Congressional Black Caucus’ next leader wants Democrats to focus on
item.description: The CBC, which was founded in 1971, will welcome a record-breaking 66 members to its ranks in the 120th Congress.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Troy Carter (D-La.) speaks during a news conference on the No Homeless Detention Centers Act on Capitol Hill on Sept. 2, 2026, in Washington.

item.dc:creator: By Cheyanne M. Daniels
item.content:encoded:
The incoming leader of the Congressional Black Caucus urged his party to focus on affordability and environmental justice in the next Congress — and the voting rights fight that ripped the party apart the last time Democrats controlled both chambers.

In an interview Tuesday, Rep. Troy Carter (D-La.) said the CBC will look to tackle affordability, health care, environmental justice, economic parity and “of course” the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act in the new Congress.

“If you ask me to order them, I would tell you they’re all going to be coming at you simultaneously,” said Carter, who is poised to become the next chair of the caucus. The Lewis bill, he added, will be “the mechanism for which all other actions flow.”

The priorities aren’t much different from what Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries touted as the party’s plans ahead of Election Day. But Democrats have looked to pass some version of voting rights legislation since the original blue wave during President Donald Trump’s first midterms, only to be stymied by Republican opposition and a brutal intraparty fight over the Senate filibuster.

Different iterations of a voting rights bill have been introduced by Democrats since 2019. While sometimes changing in size and scope, at its most expansive it would broadly remake the American elections system, from reinstating a gutted provision of the Voting Rights Act to banning partisan gerrymandering and creating public financing of congressional campaigns.

The version introduced this Congress focused specifically on the Voting Rights Act and restoring “preclearance” requirements — that states or jurisdictions with a history of discrimination get preapproval from the federal government or courts before changing voting laws — and not even more wholesale changes to the country’s election systems.

When Democrats last controlled Congress following the 2020 election, the sweeping bill passed the House amid stiff GOP opposition. It ultimately died in the Senate after then-Sens. Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) and Kyrsten Sinema (D-Ariz.) fought to keep the filibuster, effectively killing the bill, which did not have enough GOP support to clear the 60-vote threshold.

Under Democratic control, voting rights legislation has recently gotten the symbolic designation as the first piece of legislation introduced in either chamber.

Leaders within the CBC, which was founded in 1971 and is often referred to as the “conscience of the Congress” among its members, hope that the new Congress will have another opportunity to pass the bill.

The CBC projects having at least 66 members, which would be the largest caucus in its history. That number excludes some uncalled races — including Scott Colom in the deadlocked Mississippi Senate race.

The CBC’s new members in the 120th Congress will “absolutely” help the caucus push its agenda forward, including passage of the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, said Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.).

“Because we have a record number of African Americans in the Senate, we will not only be able to pass it in the House but we'll have the advocates and the individuals to put it forward to get it passed in the Senate,” Meeks, chair of the CBC’s political arm, told POLITICO.

It is not immediately clear if there is enough support to pass, particularly with the filibuster intact. A number of recently elected Democratic senators have signaled they want to keep the filibuster.

Meeks argued that the CBC’s growth was due in part to investments made by a constellation of CBC-aligned political groups. According to a memo shared with POLITICO, the groups — CBCPAC, Rolling Sea Action fund and Let it Resound — invested $20 million in races across the country, implemented a seven-figure social media creator campaign and targeted Black-led or -owned firms and media outlets for ads.

More than a dozen of their 37 targeted House races were seats held by CBC members, including Democratic Reps. Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina, who both won on maps redrawn to defeat them. Figures’ redraw came after another Supreme Court decision that further eroded the Voting Rights Act.

But the CBC, made up entirely of Democratic members, will still need to find a way to work with President Donald Trump to deliver on campaign promises. Meeks appeared unconcerned about the potential hurdle.

“The burden will be on the president,” said Meeks. “But if he continues with his tariffs, if he continues with trying to take away who we are as African Americans by trying to take away our history and destroy the legacy of our leaders, then we'll have a battle.”

item.title: New GOP campaign chairs
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Republicans in each congressional chamber picked new campaign chairs Tuesday as they plot a path back to House and Senate majorities.

Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia, a former political advisor to President Donald Trump, will take over the reins of the NRCC from Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina, who lost his election Tuesday.

Jack won a conference vote 125-53 over Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana.

Senate Republicans chose Rep. Bernie Moreno of Ohio to succeed Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina as NRSC chair. Moreno was unopposed and was approved for the job by acclamation.

item.title: USPS sounds alarm over finances, presses Congress for help
item.description: The agency says it remains in a precarious financial position despite shrinking its annual losses and cutting costs.

media:content.media:title: The American flag flies outside a U.S. Post Office branch, Monday, Nov. 24, 2025, in Boston.

item.dc:creator: By Jalen Beckford
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Postal Service is warning that it may be forced to drastically cut the number of post offices and scale back some mail services if Congress doesn’t step in to address its worsening financial troubles, with plans for reductions expected early next year.

Postmaster General David Steiner laid out the stark warning during a Board of Governors meeting Tuesday, saying the agency has few options left to shore up its finances without congressional action. The Postal Service reported a $6.5 billion net loss for fiscal 2026 on Tuesday, an improvement from its posted $9 billion loss the previous year. Still, officials warned that the agency’s financial position remains precarious.

“We will need to make drastic changes in the number of post offices and marketing mail service levels,” Steiner said. “And we will need to look at other areas to generate the cash we need to meet our obligations to our employees and to the American public.”

“We are also seeking legislative actions to establish a better and more durable business model for the Postal Service and for the benefit of the American public we serve,” he said. Steiner also noted that the agency would have fully developed plans for the potential service reductions in the first quarter of 2027, which he would present to government leaders as Congress weighs whether to intervene.

Steiner said Congress has three choices: overhaul the retirement funding requirements and other mandates weighing on USPS, provide funding to cover those obligations or accept reduced levels of service. He warned that the agency faces another impending financial cliff within five years, when its retiree health benefits fund is expected to be exhausted.

“As I've been saying in many venues, the postal service cannot be financially strong in the long term without fundamental changes to our legislatively dictated business model,” Steiner said. “We require congressional attention and action, and we require action fast,” he added, arguing that retirement costs outside the agency’s control are creating an “untenable situation” for employees.

The Postal Service has been expected to largely fund its own operations since the Postal Reorganization Act of 1970, which transformed it into an independent federal agency. Unlike most federal agencies, USPS relies primarily on revenue from postage and other services, rather than taxpayer funding.

The agency is asking Congress to raise its $15 billion borrowing cap — which hasn’t changed since 1992 — and to modify the rules that dictate how it funds retirement pension benefits. USPS also wants greater flexibility to invest retirement funds and changes to how it administers workers’ compensation claims.

Board of Governors Chair Amber McReynolds echoed the warning Tuesday, arguing that previous bipartisan efforts to overhaul the Postal Service’s finances had not gone far enough.

“Ultimately, our fiscal cliff is here,” McReynolds said. “The board continues to make uncomfortable default decisions, and we do not want to continue to operate in an unsustainable position as we have.”

McReynolds pointed to the 2022 Postal Service Reform Act — which eliminated a requirement that USPS pre-fund retiree health benefits decades in advance — as an important first step, but said other sweeping changes are needed to address the agency’s long-term financial problems.

The Postal Service has taken steps to shore up its own finances, including reducing 19 million work hours, consolidating transportation networks and raising prices. Operating revenue rose 3% to $82.9 billion, though First-Class Mail and Shipping and Packages categories saw a continued decline in volume.

Steiner said the agency has also halted nonessential hiring and suspended certain retirement contributions to conserve cash while Congress considers potential reforms. USPS deferred roughly $2.6 billion in retirement contributions this year after receiving temporary regulatory relief and suspending certain payments, but officials acknowledged those obligations will eventually be due.

“We cannot continue to jeopardize our employees’ retirement plans,” Steiner said.

Steiner took over the agency last year after Louis DeJoy resigned amid bipartisan criticism of his management of the Postal Service. Shortly before stepping down, DeJoy confirmed the agency was working alongside the Department of Government Efficiency — run at the time by Elon Musk — and announced plans to eliminate 10,000 jobs as part of efforts to reduce costs.

President Donald Trump has previously floated the idea of privatizing the Postal Service or merging it with the Commerce Department. USPS employed over 530,000 workers across the country last year.

item.title: Sanders says he won't support Schumer as majority leader
item.description: Schumer is facing pockets of opposition to lead his party, but no one has officially said they'll run against him.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) departs the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 17, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he will not support Minority Leader Chuck Schumer as leader of the Democratic caucus next year.

Sanders announced his decision at a news conference with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) shortly after Democrats huddled in their first full caucus meeting since returning to Washington following sweeping midterm election victories.

Schumer this week has begun to face pockets of opposition within his ranks, and several outside advocacy groups have weighed in against his retaking the perch. But no other senator has officially entered the race against him.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer,” Sanders (I-Vt.) said. “But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”

Slotkin added she is also a “no” on any candidate until they can articulate a plan outlining Democrats’ priorities in the first 100 days in the new Congress.

Schumer responded to Sanders' announcement during a press conference Tuesday.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader. And our caucus is really united on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war. We have great unity in our caucus and I’ll be proud to lead it as majority leader,” the New York Democrat said.

Sanders said the two senators had heard out Schumer and had a serious discussion about his ideas going forward: “Was it as definitive as it should be? In my view it was not.”

Neither senator has identified who they might support instead, though both acknowledged that Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is one name in consideration.

“We had a productive conversation,” Slotkin said of her Monday meeting with Van Hollen. “At the same time, I have the same feeling about anyone who runs as I do about Sen. Schumer. I want to see what that plan is. I want to see how it represents newer members. I will require that for anyone.”

item.title: John Thune is reelected as Senate GOP leader after midterm losses
item.description: The South Dakotan fought back efforts from some colleagues to delay leadership elections.

media:content.media:title: Senate Republican Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) walks to a Senate Republican Conference luncheon at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 10, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Senate Republicans reelected John Thune Tuesday to lead their party as it is thrust out of power in the next Congress.

The Senate GOP leadership team was reelected by acclamation inside a closed-door conference meeting that came after Republicans quashed the hopes of some conservatives to delay the leadership election.

Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) said Thune gave a “heartfelt speech” to colleagues Tuesday — with even Johnson, who was among those seeking a delay, saying the South Dakotan had been “very unfairly attacked” by the party’s base.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” he said.

Thune said in a statement after the vote that Republicans “remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats’ efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda.”

“I appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues today, and I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress,” he said.

The depth of the Senate GOP losses, however, had many senators pressing for answers on what might change inside their chamber. At least seven GOP-held seats are now in Democratic hands, with Republicans behind in two uncalled races.

“This was the worst set of losses since Watergate,” said Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, who was among the GOP senators who supported delaying the leadership elections. “I mean, it’s an incredible repudiation of the focus of this Congress.”

Members in Hawley’s camp complained this week that Republicans didn’t do enough to deliver over the past two years and that GOP senators needed more time to figure out their next steps. But Republicans overwhelmingly voted to proceed with the elections, 31-15, before choosing to keep Thune in charge.

But Thune, who remains well-liked by his GOP colleagues, was never viewed as being in jeopardy and did not face a challenger for the minority leader post. Some conservatives had hoped President Donald Trump would step in and call for Thune to go if Republicans lost the majority, but Trump instead said repeatedly that he was staying out of the leadership race.

Not even Sen. Rick Scott of Florida, who has previously run twice to lead the party in the Senate, made a bid this time around.

Thune has a challenging task ahead of him: He’ll have to manage the final two years of the Trump administration, where the president could try to keep his grip over congressional Republicans, while working to prevent further GOP losses in 2028, when the Senate map is more favorable to Democrats.

Thune also has a hefty to-do list to manage even before the majority flips in January — including avoiding a mid-December government shutdown, potentially having to deal with an impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and moving other must-pass legislation such the annual defense policy package and a farm bill.

“The job is not for the faint of heart, for sure,” Thune said Monday night. “But I feel like I’ve got something to offer and to contribute ... as we think about now having to chart a slightly new direction.”

item.title: Lisa McClain wins another term as House GOP conference chair
item.description: The Michigan lawmaker fended off a pair of challengers.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) arrives for a House Republican Conference leadership forum on Capitol Hill on Nov. 10, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan won another two years as chair of the House Republican Conference, fending off two challengers who sought to capitalize on the GOP midterm losses.

McClain won with 93 votes in a secret ballot tally over Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana, who got 57 votes, and Rep. Greg Steube of Florida, who got 27.

Houchin and Steube leaned into frustrations aired after last week’s Democratic wipeout with the state of GOP messaging, which is traditionally a focus for the conference chair position, as well as a broader desire among House Republicans for a clean leadership slate.

McClain, meanwhile, told colleagues she was ready to “get back in the fight” on their behalf.

While Houchin made the case that the GOP’s premidterm messaging was ineffective and Steube argued for a more purely conservative approach to the job, McClain pitched herself as broadly palatable to a variety of members.

“The Chair’s job is not to build a personal brand. It’s to elevate yours,” she said in the letter. “I’ll make sure you have the resources, messages, and platforms to reach your constituents and bring your voice to a national audience.”

McClain, 60, has served in Congress since 2021 and was elected conference chair two years ago, replacing Rep. Elise Stefanik of New York — who was anticipating a Trump administration appointment that never came.

item.title: Senate GOP proceeds to election
item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Senate Republicans voted 31-15 to proceed to their leadership election, effectively rejecting an attempt by conservatives to delay their leadership election.

The vote, which took place during a closed-door conference meeting Tuesday, comes after a group of conservatives — led by Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin — pushed to delay the election to give GOP senators more time to talk through the results of last week’s walloping in the midterms.

But Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who is expected to be elected to lead the party in the minority next year, questioned what would be gained by delaying the election, with no other Republicans raising their hand to run against him. Senior Republicans predicted the effort would be defeated.

item.title: Tom Emmer moves up to House GOP’s No. 2 job
item.description: His title will remain whip as Republicans go deep into the minority.

media:content.media:title: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) speaks alongside House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on March 25, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
House Republicans chose to keep Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota as party whip in the next Congress, rejecting a challenge from an ambitious younger member after last week’s sweeping midterm losses.

Emmer beat Texas Rep. August Pfluger 103-76 in the secret-ballot vote, according to two people present for the tally.

Emmer, 65, will serve alongside Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected minority leader earlier Tuesday, as House Republicans navigate the last two years of Donald Trump’s presidency and look to claw back the massive Democratic gains in 2028.

The result effectively promotes Emmer from the No. 3 spot to No. 2 spot in the House GOP leadership despite widespread frustration from members over the election results. The 48-year-old Pfluger, who has been angling for a bigger job as chair of the Republican Study Committee, argued the existing leadership echelon should have done more to protect the majority.

Emmer has served as majority whip since 2023, after helping secure a GOP majority in the 2022 midterms as NRCC chair. He launched a run for speaker later that year after California Rep. Kevin McCarthy lost the gavel and won an internal caucus vote. But President Donald Trump publicly opposed him, effectively killing his bid.

Emmer was seen at the time as a MAGA skeptic but has since become much closer to Trump. His name was floated as a potential contender for minority leader but he ultimately declined to seek the No. 1 slot several weeks before the midterms.

item.title: Jim Jordan elected House GOP leader
item.description: The Ohio Republican triumphed in his third attempt to lead Republicans on Capitol Hill.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) walks with other House members and staffers as he arrives for a House Republican Conference leadership forum on Capitol Hill on Nov. 10, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Jim Jordan will lead a much-diminished House GOP as minority leader next year, beating out Majority Leader Steve Scalise in his third attempt to lead Republicans on Capitol Hill.

Jordan won the secret ballot vote 106-73, according to two people present for the tally.

A co-founder of the House Freedom Caucus and prominent MAGA figure, Jordan pitched himself as best prepared to engage in political combat with the incoming Democratic House majority, noting he was “battle tested on the oversight front” in a letter to members. He currently chairs the House Judiciary Committee and previously chaired the Oversight Committee.

He assumes the top job after catastrophic losses for Republicans last week prompted Speaker Mike Johnson to stand down from leadership and sparked introspection in the GOP ranks about how to rebuild the party. Many viewed Jordan as a needed change of direction compared to Scalise, who has been in the top leadership ranks for more than a decade.

In brief remarks following his victory, he thanked his colleagues for their support and promised to "fight for American families."

"When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor, and on the stump every single day," he said.

Asked by reporters if he viewed his role as defending President Donald Trump, Jordan said his role is to "help House Republicans get back to the majority."

Outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson also congratulated Jordan and praised him as "a known entity, a trusted voice, a trusted leader."

"He's a fighter, and I think that's the signal that is being sent here," he said. "We are ready to dig in for the fight, and I think Jim can do a great job."

Jordan, 62, ran to be minority leader in 2018 but lost to California Rep. Kevin McCarthy, who went on to become speaker. After McCarthy was ousted from that job in 2023, Jordan tried and failed to replace him — losing a secret-ballot caucus vote to Scalise along the way.

A group of moderate Republicans kept Jordan from getting the speakership at the time, but many of those opponents will no longer serve in Congress.

Jordan had been laying the groundwork in the meanwhile to mount another run for leader, improving his fundraising and traveling widely to campaign with GOP colleagues. While Jordan needed a majority of the entire House to become speaker in 2023, he needed only a majority of the Republican conference to win the minority leader job.

It’s unclear what comes next for Scalise, who first entered the leadership ranks in 2014. He pitched himself as being best positioned to help Republicans win the majority in 2028 — something some Republicans are doubting is even possible after the blue wave last week.

item.title: Trahan crafting AI safety bill with narrower state preemption
item.description: Lawmakers in a Democrat-controlled Congress may be less likely to supersede state AI laws.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) drafted the legislation with Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.).

item.dc:creator: By Owen Dahlkamp
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Lori Trahan is revamping her artificial intelligence safety bill to narrow language preempting state laws regulating the industry, according to a person with knowledge of her efforts granted anonymity to discuss private legislative work.

Trahan’s original proposal, which the Massachusetts Democrat drafted with Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and released in June, contained preemption language that drew ire from AI safety groups. The duo substantially narrowed the provisions when they introduced the bill in August.

Democrats largely oppose blocking states from creating their own AI regulations, while the tech industry says it’s untenable to navigate a patchwork of differing laws.

Republicans, who favor preemption, will largely be on the sidelines next Congress as Democrats take over both chambers

item.title: Steve Scalise's posse
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Reps. Mario Diaz-Balart of Florida, Craig Goldman of Texas and Jeff Hurd of Colorado are set to give nominating speeches for Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise’s leadership bid this afternoon, according to a person familiar with the plans.

Diaz-Balart and Hurd are considered more moderate House Republicans, and both narrowly won reelection last week. Scalise is making the case he is better positioned than hard-right rival Jim Jordan to lead the GOP back to the majority.

“I can go to the most ruby-red or the most swing district,” Scalise said leaving the candidate forum. “We’re going to have to go back to those swing districts we lost, and we’ll get those back.”

item.title: GOP senators take a break
item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
After about two hours of private discussion about last week's midterm losses and the path forward, Senate Republicans plan to reconvene at 2 p.m. to continue with electing their leaders, according to several GOP senators.

Members will attend committee meetings and a conference lunch before regathering inside the Capitol. They haven’t yet voted on a request to delay the election. If it is rejected, elections would proceed later Tuesday.

item.title: House Oversight Republicans release final report on Epstein investigation
item.description: Democrats, however, say the inquiry into the federal government’s handling of the case is “just getting started.”

media:content.media:title: House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) walks to speak with reporters before a closed interview with Lesley Groff, a former assistant to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, on Capitol Hill on June 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Republicans on the House Oversight Committee released a report Tuesday morning wrapping up their 15-month investigation into Jeffrey Epstein and how the federal government handled the criminal case against him.

Among their findings: President Donald Trump was not implicated in Epstein’s sex trafficking operation; Epstein’s abuse of young women and girls continued for years because of repeated failures from law enforcement and federal prosecutors; and the Justice Department failed to “adequately communicate” around the public release of the so-called Epstein files.

“Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims,” Oversight Chair James Comer of Kentucky, who will step down as the top Republican on the panel in January due to GOP Conference term limit rules, said in a statement. “Governments at every level and powerful institutions must meet their legal obligations to identify these crimes, stop perpetrators, and deliver justice for survivors.”

The 136-page report notes that the “the Committee’s investigation was prompted by the decades-long failures of individuals and institutions charged with protecting vulnerable survivors and holding powerful offenders accountable” — though it was actually compelled to launch an inquiry after Oversight Committee members voted in July 2025 to force the panel to subpoena Epstein documents DOJ was at that point continuing to withhold.

From there, the committee went on to interview some of the most powerful individuals within Epstein’s business, financial or social orbit, including Bill and Hillary Clinton, Bill Gates, Leon Black and Les Wexner. Members also had a chance to question Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and ex-Attorney General Pam Bondi.

The findings of Comer’s report takes some aim at the Justice Department, which oversaw a haphazard release of the Epstein files last year in compliance with a law Congress passed in November 2025. It recommends DOJ establish a proper process for Epstein survivors to access their personal files without redactions, and that the agency work to ensure that federal investigators interview or reinterview key witnesses of those harmed by Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein’s co-conspirator now serving a 20 year federal prison sentence.

DOJ also needs to ensure there is rigorous enforcement of policies in place to prevent conflicts of interest in investigations and prosecutions. Separately, the Treasury Department and its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network must review whether financial institutions are meeting their reporting requirements to prevent suspicious activities like human trafficking, which Epstein was able to finance through his business ties.

Spokespeople for the Justice and Treasury Departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Democrats, who plan to continue the investigation in the new Congress, have been deeply critical of the GOP-led inquiry — including accusing Comer of not demanding more witnesses be compelled to testify under oath and on camera. They also have already released materials to more tightly tie Trump to Epstein’s crimes, with calls for a special counsel to be appointed to investigate that potential link.

Comer’s report lays out as one key finding that “Oversight Democrats concentrated their investigative efforts on President Trump rather than the broader, decades long institutional failures that enabled Epstein’s abuse and robbed survivors of swift justice.”

Trump has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein’s actions and has repeatedly said he and Epstein had a falling out years ago and that he banned Epstein from Mar-a-Lago “for being a creep.”

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the leading Democrat on the Oversight Committee, in a statement slammed the report as “based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein.”

“We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation,” Garcia said. “We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started.”

item.title: Senior Dems will make life ‘hell’ without Jeffries vote, freshman rep says
item.description: Rep.-elect Don Leonard said he will not vote for Rep. Hakeem Jeffries without a commitment to address Citizens United and U.S. aid to Israel.

media:content.media:title: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries calls on a reporter during a press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Casey He
item.content:encoded:
An incoming member of Congress said senior House Democrats have vowed to make his life “a living hell” and oust him in 2028 if he does not support Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’ speaker bid.

Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) said in a social media post that the senior members told him to vote for Jeffries regardless of whether the Democratic leader commits to addressing key issues, including a constitutional amendment to overturn the Citizens United decision and ending U.S. support for Israel and the war in Iran.

“It's part of the stuff you see in the movies,” said Leonard. “It's a whole other thing when it's in person, by people who actually care about you and are cheering for you but expect you to wear the team jersey and be a good team player.”

He added that he received a letter from Jeffries that “still left several of my constituents’ questions unanswered.”

Leonard, who last week flipped an Ohio district long held by Republicans, said separately in an interview with Joy Reid that he would not vote for Jeffries unless the Democratic leader commits to addressing his demands on Israel and campaign finance.

“So unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation's laws, like the Leahy Law, against Israeli genocide in Gaza; unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis, which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the incoming lawmaker said in a clip he also posted on his social media.

Jeffries’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. At a Monday news conference, the longtime Israel backer said he plans to have many conversations with his caucus in the coming days.

“I’m going to work hard to talk to every single member about what we’ve been able to do together over the last two years, and what the opportunities are for us to do together in the next two years, to deliver upon the dramatic change that the American people so decisively voted for,” he said.

Leonard’s remarks come as House Democrats are gearing up for a speaker nomination vote next week. Jeffries is expected to cruise to victory, as his party’s sizable new majority means he can afford at least three dozen defections.

Asked about Leonard’s comments on Tuesday, Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), who’s running unopposed for House majority whip, said he doesn’t know which senior Democrats Leonard was referring to. Aguilar also credited Jeffries for playing “an integral part” in House Democrats’ sweep last week.

“It's my belief that he will be overwhelmingly selected to lead this caucus. I don't lose any sleep over that,” he said. “Members could have ideas and interests, and they could have asks along the way, but the outcome is not in question.”

Jeffries’ allies have said they want the party united behind his speakership so it can focus on addressing issues key to voters instead of being consumed by factional warfare.

Still, not all Democratic members have committed to supporting Jeffries, with some progressives hoping to use the speaker election to work through internal divisions ahead of the new Congress next year.

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

item.title: GOP nominating speeches
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
House GOP leadership candidates are lining up colleagues to give nominating speeches ahead of today’s elections.

Rep. Ben Cline of Virginia said he will nominate Texas Rep. August Pfluger for whip this morning. Cline is set to take over the chair of the Republican Study Committee from Pfluger. Rep. Nathaniel Moran will also give a speech for his fellow Texan.

Rep. Carlos Gimenez of Florida said in an interview he will speak on behalf of Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym, who is running for NRCC chair, and Rep. Julie Fedorchak of North Dakota will give a speech for Utah Rep. Blake Moore, who is running unopposed to keep his position as conference vice chairman.

Speaker Mike Johnson said in an interview he will not be speaking on behalf of any candidate.

item.title: RNC members call for delay in congressional leadership elections after midterm losses
item.description: Their public demand for accountability is another sign of the pressure facing Republicans in the aftermath of the bloodbath.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jim Jordan.

item.dc:creator: By Erin Doherty
item.content:encoded:
Dozens of Republican National Committee members want congressional Republicans to delay their leadership elections by at least 30 days, arguing that the party must reckon with its widespread midterm losses first.

“There is no way to sugarcoat what happened on Election Day. From coast to coast, and in some of the reddest parts of the country, Republicans were humiliated,” the 31 RNC members — from 21 states and two territories — wrote in a letter shared with POLITICO. Now is not the time, they argue, to “accept the status quo” — it’s time “do some serious soul-searching.”

“We ... urge the House and Senate Republican Conferences to postpone leadership elections for at least 30 days to allow for an initial assessment of the November 3 losses, a substantive discussion of what went wrong, and an opportunity for leadership candidates to explain how they intend to address those failures,” the members write.

The House and Senate GOP are both set to hold elections Tuesday to decide their next slate of leaders, with candidate forums scheduled to begin this morning. A handful of senators, including Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), have also called for a delay following last week’s elections.

In the House, Speaker Mike Johnson will not take the top post again, leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan to battle it out. John Thune is expected to be reelected as the No.1 GOP leader in the Senate.

While the elections appear likely to proceed as scheduled, the letter underscores the brewing discontent within the GOP following last week’s wipe out — including even among some of its most loyal members. Democrats won their largest majority in both chambers in decades and the Republican Party has a lot of work to do to resolve its divisions and overcome President Donald Trump’s unpopularity with voters.

“Rushing these elections before examining what happened risks protecting the very leaders whose decisions need to be examined,” the RNC members wrote. “Accountability must come before leadership elections.”

Amy Kremer, Georgia’s national committeeperson and one of the letter’s signatories, also pressed congressional Republicans to show what they intend to accomplish before choosing their next slate of leaders.

“The people who knock on doors, make the calls, and give their hard-earned money are owed more than business as usual. Before leadership asks for another two years in charge, show us what they intend to deliver in the lame-duck session,” she told POLITICO. “What is the plan to pass the SAVE America Act and move pending confirmations? Our voters deserve specifics and results.”

The RNC faces its own leadership fight after last week’s losses. KC Crosbie, the RNC co-chair, wrote in a letter to members last week that she has “decided to run for chair” of the committee, challenging the Trump-picked Joe Gruters. One day later, the president praised Gruters on his Truth Social, and said “I know he will do an incredible job in 2028.”

item.title: Capitol agenda: GOP leaders face a post-rout reckoning
item.description: The House and Senate GOP are poised to hold separate elections Tuesday to decide who will serve as the top Republicans in the next Congress.

media:content.media:title: Senate Republican Leader John Thune speaks with reporters as he departs a briefing on Capitol Hill on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Republican leaders are fighting to keep their power on Capitol Hill Tuesday after stunning midterm losses last week.

The House and Senate GOP are poised to hold separate elections Tuesday to decide who will serve as the top Republicans in the next Congress. The winners are expected to immediately start charting a course back to governing relevance after Democrats gained the largest majorities won by any party in decades and voters delivered a firm rebuke of President Donald Trump.

How it’ll go: House Republicans will hold a candidate forum at 9 a.m. to hear from members running for all leadership positions, and a secret ballot will begin at 1:30 p.m.

Senate Republicans will meet at 9 a.m. It’s unclear how long their forum will continue — with some members pushing for a vote to delay the election to give more time for deliberations. But senior Republicans expect that push to fail and to know who will lead the conference by the end of the day.

What to expect: The House elections will pit existing Republican leaders vying to keep their top spots against insurgents who are hoping to capitalize on a desire from some for a clean slate.

Speaker Mike Johnson is bowing out, leaving Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan to battle it out for the No. 1 perch.

Jordan is pledging a fresh look for the House GOP’s top echelon and has swiped at Johnson and Scalise for having too often “operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us.”

Scalise is seeking to fend off the throw-the-bums-out sentiment by drawing on his experience as a fundraiser and a set of personal relationships he has closely tended for years.

Thune appears to be on a path to reelection today as Senate GOP leader, despite calls from a handful of senators, like Sen. Ron Johnson for a delay. One benchmark to watch: Sixteen Republicans voted for a similar delay in 2022, when Mitch McConnell sought his final term as leader.

Thune said Monday Republicans will be given plenty of space to talk through how they are feeling after the midterms. He’s pitching himself as ready to lead the conference amid an uncertain final two years of the Trump administration and a lot of 2028 jockeying.

“The job is not for the faint of heart, for sure,” Thune told POLITICO on Monday. “But I feel like I’ve got something to offer and to contribute ... as we think about now having to chart a slightly new direction.”

What else we’re watching: 

— GOP BUCKS TRUMP ON NVIDIA: Senior Republican lawmakers are considering investigating Nvidia over CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, putting Trump’s strong defense of the tech titan at odds with mounting scrutiny from members of his own party. GOP chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China committees are asking Huang to appear at a closed-door briefing next week that could lay the groundwork for an investigation into Nvidia. Other Republicans are now calling for Congress or other federal authorities to launch probes into Huang’s conduct and Nvidia’s broader dealings with China, arguing the situation is a serious national security risk.

— PERMITTING DEAL DEBATE LAUNCHES: The lead senators negotiating an energy permitting deal are now promising a “healthy amendment process” after the legislation cleared an initial hurdle Monday. Nearly all Senate Republicans and more than a dozen Democrats voted yesterday to advance the bipartisan permitting reform bill. Several of the Democrats who voted to advance the legislation were still critical of it — with some like Sens. Chuck Schumer and Catherine Cortez Masto pushing for further changes to the bill as the voting process continues.

Mia McCarthy, Jordain Carney, Christine Mui, Ari Hawkins, Gabby Miller, Sophia Cai, Owen Dahlkamp, Katherine Long and Nico Portuondo contributed to this report.

item.title: A blue wave complicates the math in New York’s redistricting push
item.description: State Democrats will need to revisit whether a costly push to allow gerrymandering is still a priority.

media:content.media:title: Voters cast their ballots at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Bill Mahoney
item.content:encoded:
ALBANY, New York — Top New York Democrats still want to redraw the state’s congressional maps before 2028. But after Tuesday’s blue wave, their plans might not be as set in stone as they were a few months ago.

President Donald Trump successfully backed redistricting plans in several red states during his second term. The aggressive push led Democrats to respond with their own tit-for-tat efforts. But redistricting in Republican dominated states did not yield the desired results for the GOP — as evidenced by Tuesday’s blue wave — leading leaders from both parties to rethink their approach.

“It is a matter that will certainly be the subject of serious discussion in the Assembly Democratic conference,” said state Assemblymember Charles Lavine, who carries the legislation that would allow for mid-decade changes to the map. “It’s certainly a possibility — a strong possibility, I would say, but I cannot predict what the conference’s position will be.”

New York has been a prime target for Democrats as they’ve engaged in a national redistricting war. Gerrymandered maps could have helped the party flip four congressional seats this cycle.

But the urgency of acting on such a plan diminished a bit on Tuesday night. Democrats flipped one of those four seats, thanks to Cait Conley’s defeat of Rep. Mike Lawler. And Republican gerrymanders backfired elsewhere in the country, translating into a massive majority for Democrats, even without additional New York pickups.

Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mickie Sherrill, from a neighboring blue state,said after the election she will no longer pursue mid-decade changes.

New York Democrats aren’t going that far — at least not yet. Rep. Joe Morelle, who has been the go-between for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and top Democrats at the state level, said “the principals still remain.”

“That hyperpartisan gerrymandering left New York at a decided disadvantage because we couldn’t do mid-term redistricting,” he said. “I will still advocate for moving ahead, and I think other people will as well.”

Redistricting has never been without risks. State lawmakers approved a constitutional amendment this spring to allow for changes. If they do so again in 2027, it will appear on the ballot as a referendum next November.

That ballot question fight will be costly for both sides, plausibly topping $100 million. And it could provide Republicans with an urgently-needed impetus to show up to the polls — reducing the chances that New York Democrats will carry this year’s momentum into 2027’s local elections and eradicate the GOP bench.

“Opposition to this type of amendment can drive out Republicans and common-sense Democrats,” said Assemblymember-elect Marc Molinaro, a Republican who has previously won local races and a congressional term.

This week’s elections “proved” that gerrymandering can backfire, Molinaro said. “In districts that Republicans in other states drew to their benefit, Republicans were trounced.”

That lesson could indeed make some Democrats a bit more hesitant once the dust settles.

Take a region with three districts that are 60 percent Republican and one that’s 60 percent Democratic. That can be redrawn to have four districts that are each 55 percent Republican. That’s a gain of one GOP seat on paper — but it shrinks the breathing room in the others, creating the possibility that each of the four seats is vulnerable in a wave year.

Detailed results of this year’s congressional races in states with Republican gerrymanders like Florida and Texas will soon provide vivid examples of how such maneuvers can backfire in exactly that fashion. And the math in New York isn’t that different.

The New York maps could allow for a new Democratic-friendly district upstate. Rep. Tim Kennedy received 65% of the vote this year, Rep. Paul Tonko got 64%, and Morelle polled at 63%. Reducing the Democratic margins in a couple of those would allow for either Rep. Claudia Tenney’s seat or the district won by Republican Anthony Constantino to be made bluer — but it could also make the currently safe Democrats vulnerable if the political pendulum swings back in 2028 or 2030.

Another Democratic pickup opportunity is on Long Island, where the party has spent years fantasizing about turning the four congressional districts from a 2-2 map to one with a 3-1 edge.

The party improved a bit in those districts this year. But the margins were far from overwhelming — Democratic nominees received 56.7%, 55.2%, 48.9%, and 48.8% of the vote. There’s room to blend those existing seats into districts that increase the odds in one of the GOP districts — but nowhere near enough to guarantee the costly fight would result in a pick-up, especially in a non-wave year.

There are, to be sure, other advantages to gerrymandering. The party could blend the seat won by Conley with Rep. George Latimer’s dark blue district to make both of them locks in the future.

And there is the prize of GOP Rep. Nicole Malliotakis’ Staten Island seat. She received 56% of the vote this year. Her district, surrounded by a sea of Brooklyn and Manhattan seats where Democrats topped 75%, could easily be chopped up and reconfigured with a dark blue shade.

That’s been the top priority for pro-gerrymandering Democrats all decade — the party unsuccessfully sought to use the courts to force a new Staten Island map just this year. That impulse hasn’t changed.

“Staten Island, the people there basically have no choice,” Morelle said. “They don’t really have a way to impact the people who represent them.”

But the state Legislature will ultimately need to decide whether pick-up opportunities like the Malliotakis seat are still worth a fight that’s likely to drown out everything else in New York next year.

“I am personally supportive,” Lavine said. “But because I am only a legislator and not a ruler, I will work with the majority opinion of my colleagues.”

item.title: House Republicans could be about to clean their own house
item.description: The minority leader contest between Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise will test just how clean of a slate lawmakers want ahead of 2028.

media:content.media:title: Lisa McClain (left) and Steve Scalise (right) are facing doubts from members who want to move cleanly past Mike Johnson's speakership.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
One week after suffering devastating midterm losses, Republicans in the House will decide just how thoroughly to clean their own house.

While Speaker Mike Johnson is exiting the scene in January, Tuesday’s GOP leadership elections will still pit members of the existing leadership structure against insurgents who are hoping to capitalize on the desire for a clean slate.
