“Somebody’s got to get fired,” said Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.), who said he is backing outsiders in the three top races “because we got our butts handed to us.”

At the top of that slate is Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, a 20-year House veteran and a well-known face of the GOP’s hard-right wing who nevertheless has never served in the senior leadership ranks. He is facing off for minority leader against Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the sitting majority leader who has held the party’s No. 2 or No. 3 slot since 2014.

Jordan is pledging a fresh look for the House GOP’s top echelon and has swiped at Johnson and Scalise for having too often “operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us.”

But Scalise is seeking to fend off the throw-the-bums-out sentiment by drawing on his experience as a fundraiser and a set of personal relationships he has closely tended — some for a decade or more. He’s expected to benefit as well from the distrust of Jordan held in some pockets of the conference.

His pitch to members has been relatively simple: that he is battle-tested from one Democratic takeover, in 2018, and is best equipped to do it again.

Rep. Mike Haridopolos of Florida said he saw no “bad options” on the leadership ticket but said he was convinced Scalise knows “how to go from the minority to the majority” and also has long experience going head-to-head with Democrats on the floor.

“I think we need, more than ever, clarity of message and clarity of, this is what our agenda will be,” he said in an interview.

The old-vs.-new dynamic is at play in downballot races, as well. Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota is looking to remain GOP whip, effectively moving from the No. 3 to No. 2 spot in the new Republican minority. He’s up against Rep. August Pfluger, an ambitious Texan who chairs the conservative Republican Study Committee — a well-known steppingstone for leadership aspirants.

Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan is similarly looking to stay as Republican conference chair, which will be the No. 3 post, but faces competition from Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida. They are looking to capitalize on grumbling about McClain’s handling of party messaging.

Stutzman — who is backing Pfluger and Houchin in addition to Jordan — said the scale of the GOP losses argued for complete turnover in the senior party ranks: “There's got to be a change. Look at college football. I mean, if you lose, coaches get fired.”

Several other House Republicans who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak frankly about the secret-ballot race also said they wanted a fresh start — especially after Johnson, Scalise and Emmer centered the GOP’s case for reelection on a policy bill passed more than a year ago.

“We didn't drive a good strong agenda, and I think Jordan is pointing that out,” one of them said. “He is a very good standard-bearer for conservative policies, and he's quite credible all over the country in advocating for that.”

That’s not to say every Republican’s decision is coming down to old guard vs. new, with some saying in interviews they were planning to split their tickets. Some said they would support Jordan and Emmer, while others also said they were voting for Scalise and Pfluger.

Tuesday’s winners are expected to start charting a course back to governing relevance as Democrats enjoy the largest House majority won by any party in more than 30 years. They will also have to navigate the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency after voters delivered a firm rebuke of his leadership over the past two years.

Trump has not taken sides in the race, nor has Johnson.

"We have two extraordinary guys that are running to lead the conference," the outgoing speaker said Monday. "We'll see how that shakes out."

Neither Jordan or Scalise has telegraphed any plans to separate the House GOP from the unpopular president, and most GOP members said that debate would play out on the presidential campaign trail — not on Capitol Hill.

Instead, they said, they wanted their new leaders to focus on positioning the party for a return to the House majority and clawing back some of the 42-and-counting seats they lost to Democrats this year.

“The point of being in the minority is to get to the majority,” Rep. Nick LaLota of New York, who narrowly eked out a win in his Long Island district and declined to say who he would support.

Others have concluded that what happened last week was simply not House leaders’ fault.

“There are people who are going to blame the losses last week on leadership or bad messaging or whatever,” said Rep. Mike Simpson of Idaho, who is backing the three sitting leaders. “The reality is, there's nothing that we could have done that could have stopped this blue tsunami.”

item.title: Some Democrats want more than a Hakeem Jeffries victory. They want a blowout.
item.description: “We can't have months and months of acrimony,” said Rep.-elect Dan Koh.

media:content.media:title: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
Hakeem Jeffries’ supporters don’t just want him to win — they want him to win big.

The massive Democratic House victory last week has transformed what might have otherwise been a fraught effort for the sitting minority leader to secure the speaker’s gavel, where a smaller majority could have empowered a tightknit block of hard-left holdouts. Now a broader group is intent on sending a message.

“The people want to see unity,” Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana said in an interview. “They don't want to see fighting. They don't want to see infighting. They want to see the level of togetherness to advance an agenda.”

The good feelings surrounding Democrats’ House gains have quieted the debate about the leadership of the caucus, however large it might be. As counting continues and operatives hold out hope for 260 seats — the largest majority for any party since 1993 — progressive activists continue to call for an alternative to Jeffries.

While no sitting or incoming lawmaker has announced outright opposition, several who ran on populist economic platforms are withholding endorsements.

“I want to see who the other options are and what their agendas are, so that we can make sure that it aligns with the needs of my congressional district,” said Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack of North Carolina.

On Capitol Hill, Jeffries’ allies aren’t fretting about the ultimate outcome — he can afford at least three dozen defections — but his allies are now working to unify Democrats ahead of a nominating vote next week and an official tally on the House floor in early January.

“The American people want us to focus in on issues of affordability,” Rep. Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, the incoming Rules Committee chair, said in an interview. “That's what I heard: affordability, affordability, affordability. So let's get on with the business of electing Hakeem as speaker, and let's focus in on what this election was all about.”

The chaotic past four years of GOP rule are hanging over the vote. Hamstrung by relatively tiny majorities, GOP leaders struggled to keep unruly factions in step — often resulting in dramatic confrontations. In 2023, a group of discontented Republicans voted out a speaker for the first time, putting the deposed Kevin McCarthy into the history books.

Many Democrats said they are intent on setting the tone early that this majority will be functional and productive, not constantly racked by factional warfare.

“I don't believe that we can have the kind of acrimony that we had under Kevin McCarthy and the Republicans,” Rep.-elect Dan Koh of Massachusetts told reporters Sunday. “We need to learn from MAGA. … We need to get to the bottom of [President Donald] Trump's corruption and lower costs for people. We can't have months and months of acrimony.”

Jeffries boasts strong backing around the caucus, with power bases in the Congressional Black Caucus, which is projected to have more than 60 members next term, and the New Democrat Coalition, which is tracking toward more than 140 members. While there is overlap between those two groups and there could be defections, support from these two groups alone already puts Jeffries close to the 218 votes he would need in January.

Plenty of top progressives are endorsing Jeffries, too. Rep. Greg Casar of Texas, the Congressional Progressive Caucus chair, is voting for him, as is the group’s influential former chair, Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, perhaps the best-known face of the party’s leftist wing, is also backing Jeffries and whipped out a whiteboard on a recent livestream to explain to her massive social-media following how the speaker election works.

Not everyone is on board. A handful of new members, many but not all of whom are progressive, reaffirmed this weekend that they are as yet uncommitted to Jeffries.

“I have a lot to consider,” moderate Rep.-elect Zack Mullock of New Jersey said Sunday. “But it'll be an important decision that I'm going to talk to a lot of people who know a lot more than I do.”

Outside critics are hoping the noncommittals mean there’s an opening to block Jeffries’ ascension — or at least win concessions. Some leading progressives are framing the upcoming votes as a chance to resolve, or at least talk through, certain internally divisive issues before Democrats enter the majority.

Rep. Ro Khanna of California cited “Medicare for All” health care policy and the U.S. relationship with Israel as particular flashpoints.

“It’s a healthy process to have that conversation,” he said. “I think we will advance some of those policies that people voted for, and I'm part of those conversations.”

Jeffries said Monday he would be having plenty of personal conversations in the coming days.

“I'm going to work hard to talk to every single member about what we've been able to do together over the last two years, and what the opportunities are for us to do together in the next two years, to deliver upon the dramatic change that the American people so decisively voted for,” he said at a news conference.

The members of the new Congress, both incumbent and incoming, will vote on a speaker nomination next week, which requires only a simple majority of Democrats. The tougher test is on the floor in January, where a speaker must win a majority of all 435 members.

One recent benchmark is the backlash Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California faced after Democrats retook the majority in 2018, in the middle of Trump’s first term. After being elected speaker with zero internal opposition in 2007 and 2009, 32 Democrats opposed her comeback in the caucus vote, and 15 ultimately voted for another candidate or recorded themselves as “present” on the floor — barely allowing her to eke through.

But the caucus largely united behind Pelosi as she subsequently battled with Trump, and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina — who was No. 3 leader under Pelosi — said it was not important that every Democrat be in lockstep.

“I don't know why everybody thinks you got to be unanimous,” he said. “You can have unity and not be unanimous.”

Mia McCarthy contributed to this report.

item.title: Machinists union calls on Schumer to step aside as leader
item.description: The letter comes ahead of the Senate Democrats’ first big meeting to discuss next steps on electing their new majority leader.

media:content.media:title: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) speaks with reporters as he walks to his office at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Will Steakin and Dasha Burns
item.dc:contributor: By Will Steakin and Dasha Burns
item.content:encoded:
A major labor union is telling Sen. Chuck Schumer it’s time to go.

The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers sent the New York lawmaker a letter Monday urging him “not to seek another term” as Senate Democratic leader — making the 600,000-member union the latest voice to join the push for a leadership shakeup after last week’s elections.

“After thoughtful discussions with our IAM Union Executive Council, we believe this is the right moment for a new generation to lead Senate Democrats,” the letter reads.

“This week’s elections sent a clear message: working people are demanding change,” IAM International President Brian Bryant wrote in the letter, which was copied to the full Senate Democratic Caucus and obtained by POLITICO.

The letter adds that the moment “will require fresh ideas, new energy and a new generation of leadership.”

In a statement to POLITICO, Bryant was even more blunt: “The IAM Union is through with any member of leadership, in any political party, who stops one iota short of being a ferocious, unyielding and unbending champion of working people.”

Schumer’s office declined to comment. A Senate Democratic aide, granted anonymity to speak candidly, called the letter "a counterproductive move against ... a longtime IAM ally and a steadfast champion of labor."

In his letter, Bryant thanked Schumer for a decade atop the Senate Democratic Caucus and called him “a trusted friend of organized labor.” But he also urged returning and newly elected Democratic senators to pick a “consensus leader” through “a fair and open process,” and laid out a to-do list for whoever gets the job.

That list includes passing a rail safety bill and the PRO Act, which would make it easier for workers to unionize, as well as restoring bargaining rights for federal workers and reviving enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies Republicans allowed to expire. The Senate Democratic aide noted it the machinists' opposition to Schumer for leader was "particularly puzzling given his longstanding commitment to passing the PRO Act."

The letter lands on the eve of the first full Senate Democratic Caucus meeting since the midterms. That meeting will be where Democrats begin to chart the course for electing their next majority leader, with some now saying it might be time to write a new chapter for party leadership — especially looking ahead to 2028.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.)said Monday night that he still considering a challenge to Schumer, while Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) reiterated she wants to hear Schumer’s vision for how he’d lead the party over the next two years before she pledges him her support.

item.title: Chris Van Hollen not closing the door on Schumer challenge
item.description: The Maryland Democrat is also eyeing a presidential run in 2028.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) speaks during a press conference on newly filed Iran war powers resolutions at the U.S. Capitol, on April 13, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney and Calen Razor
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney and Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen told reporters Monday evening that he’s in “listening mode” about a potential bid for majority leader — and isn't yet ruling out running against Chuck Schumer.

“What I've said from the very beginning is we shouldn't have a coronation,” said Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, adding that he “hasn't shut the door.”

Van Hollen’s comments come as Schumer, the current minority leader, is widely expected to be elected to lead the new Senate majority in January. But some Democrats have held off on saying they would vote for the New York lawmaker, arguing they first want clarity on what the party’s strategy will be for the next two years.

Democrats will meet as a group Tuesday to start talking about their path forward.

Van Hollen met with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) on Monday, after she declined over the weekend to rule out her own leadership ambitions. Slotkin reiterated Monday that she will not vote for a majority leader candidate who cannot articulate a plan, especially for the first 100 days.

“I think a lot of members are calling each other and talking to each other and saying the same thing,” Slotkin said.

Both Van Hollen and Slotkin are viewed as potential presidential contenders. Van Hollen, asked previously about speculation that he could run for leader, had suggested that his focus was on 2028 and making sure Democrats win back the White House.

Schumer may not need these two lawmakers to win his leadership election, however: He only needs a majority of his caucus to support him during a closed-door meeting to be convened in early December.

Plenty of Senate Democrats appear more than happy to vote for Schumer after the party exceeded expectations in last week's midterms. Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said Monday he's one of them.

“I plan to continue to support Schumer just as I have, but I'm also very excited about the new ideas and energy that the new members will bring,” said Blumenthal. “We need them and we need to listen to them and the Senate needs to change the way it operates.”

item.title: Jeffries pushes to restrict China chip exports in defense bill
item.description: The post-election push comes as Nvidia investigates an alleged Chinese spy effort targeting its CEO.

media:content.media:title: Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks with reporters during a news conference in Washington on Monday.

item.dc:creator: By Jalen Beckford and Riley Rogerson
item.dc:contributor: By Jalen Beckford and Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says he’ll push to use the annual defense policy bill to tighten restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, an effort gaining momentum amid the revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.


"There are provisions currently in the Senate version of the NDAA that will restrict chip access to China that I strongly support, and I think we're going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version of the National Defense Authorization,” Jeffries told reporters Monday.

The House Democratic leader’s comments came a day after Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Jeffries’ backing gives a bipartisan Senate push more support in the House as Democrats prepare to take control of the House and Senate following the party’s strong midterm showing.

The Senate legislation, the AI Overwatch Act, would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China and other countries of concern. Other provisions would help track where exported chips end up and tighten restrictions on sales of the equipment used to make them.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) also called Monday for Congress to include the AI Overwatch Act in the defense bill, citing reports that Nvidia had secured approval to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to its military.

“NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related,” the senators wrote in a statement.
